Introduction

Liber Octo Quaestionum ad Maximilianum Caesarem — "A Book of Eight Questions to Emperor Maximilian" — is Trithemius's answer to the eight questions Maximilian set him: on faith and reason, on the faith necessary for salvation, on the miracles of unbelievers, on witches and harmful magic, and on related matters. Composed in 1508, it is his principal statement on witchcraft and had a long reception in early-modern demonology, furnishing later writers with both argument and authority. The questions are enumerated at the head of the book and answered in turn, in the same blend of scholastic reasoning and pastoral judgement that marks Trithemius's shorter treatises.

This is the 1601 Mainz edition (Albinus; Herzog August Bibliothek scan, distributed under a CC BY-SA licence at source) — the second of two print witnesses of the Octo Quaestionum in this corpus, alongside the 1534 Cologne edition (prdl-32286). The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. No complete English translation of the work has been published; only excerpts have appeared in English. The Latin of this witness is clean and the translation sits in the top tier (S).

Epigram of Richard Sbrulius of Forum Julii.

Who would deny that there is a God, parent of heaven and earth? No one is so savage as to deny that there is a God. God himself is everywhere venerated throughout the whole world, but he is nevertheless sought by a different path. The barbarian worships him as moving all things by fixed law; the Turk denies the holy Son and Spirit. The Hebrew boasts that he holds the true doctrines, and thinks that, with Moses as guide, he is the race of God. But the people of Christ, who took their name from his name, steadfastly proclaim that God is triune. The greatest Maximilian, who presides over the empire, continually aids the cause and honor of Christ. He asks, as it is right for an august king to ask such things, why the highest God permits there to be so many sects; why he does not show himself equally to all mortals; why he wished many things to lie hidden under hard signs. In order, Father Trithemius unfolds all things to the King, he the leader and glory of the hooded flock. Whoever you are who used to doubt concerning the holy faith, read this: soon you will be a sure pupil of Christ. The end.

I. On Faith and Understanding. First Question.

The first question of your Most Serene Majesty was this: why almighty God wished to be believed by mortals rather than known and understood, that is, by the mode of cognition and understanding by which he is known and understood by the holy angels.

I remember that I answered this question, posed before me by your most sacred Majesty, as follows. Almighty God, who is without beginning, pure intellect, eternal and unchangeable, existing above every [unclear], far more perfect than we are with infinite perfections, by his most ample will created from nothing two intellects in the beginning, namely the angelic and the human. The angelic intellect, at the beginning of its condition, was made in the actuality of all things [unclear], and moved all things. The human intellect, however, at first consists indeed in the potentiality of all things, but is ignorant of all things. In the end, however, through many and continual actions, it will again become like the angelic, knowing both God and all things that pertain to the cognition of the aforesaid cognition and understanding.

The angelic and human intellects differ as any two opposites do: namely as act and potency, light and darkness, knowledge and ignorance, possession and privation, beginning and end, immobile and mobile, substance and accident, truth and likeness, nature and art, health and infirmity, whole and part. For the angelic intellect is as act, light, knowledge, possession, beginning, immobile, immediate, simple, substance, truth, nature, whole. The human, however, is as potency, darkness, ignorance, privation, end, mobile, mediated, composite, accident, likeness, art, part. Hence whatever belongs to the angelic intellect from the beginning, these same things afterwards belong to the human from the end, when it has laid aside the burden of flesh; for just as the beginning, nature, perfects the angelic, so the end, art, after many exercises, raises the human upward.

Wherefore, between these two intellects there is the greater inequality from the beginning; yet in the end they are at last made equal, where the human intellect will be as great by art as the angelic had previously been by nature. Hence it is clear that the angelic intellect, as soon as it was created, from the beginning, without any action or motion of its own, immovably and substantially by nature knew all things that it can understand, and that in an instant, created full and perfect with the knowledge of all things, it came forth. But the human intellect, because it was created in the ignorance and privation of all things, and was temporally destined, for its exercise, into the body, must by continual action, motion, and art arrive at knowledge of God and of all things. It will finally equal the angelic, the end changing its potentiality into act, and making it, as it passes from the merely potential and possible into essence, full from empty, perfect from imperfect, possessing from deprived, luminous from dark, diurnal from nocturnal, solar from lunar, from earthly [unclear] cannot, that is, as Christophilus Paul says: as long as we are in the flesh, we are absent from the Lord, to know God [continues].

To Emperor Maximilian.

The intellect is pure, simple, and perfect; but the human intellect, so long as it remains in the body, is impure, mixed, unstable, and imperfect, and for this reason, without faith, wholly ignorant of the knowledge of God and of heavenly things. The object of both intellects, namely both the human and the angelic, is the same: that highest and unchangeable good, God, the single principle of all things, to which they return by a natural desire for knowledge. But if the angelic intellect is compared with the human, it is as nature is to art, and as intellect simply speaking is to reason, which touches upon the principles of the disciplines; reason, however, runs from principles to conclusions. Hence it is manifest that the angelic intellect apprehends its proper object immovably; toward that object the human intellect, by means of the angelic, after many exercises of itself, as has been said, at length, by reasoning, prepares assent for itself.

The human intellect, however, is separated, by the mediation of the angelic, from the perfection of knowledge of its natural object, and therefore necessarily becomes movable, returning by means of it to its own principle. For every motion proceeds from an extreme through a mean to an extreme. But where there is no mean, the extremes are already immediate, proximate, and for that reason immovable. The human intellect, set as it were in a dark prison, so long as it is held in the body, is moved by sense and reason toward understanding, although confusedly, imperfectly, and less fully; and therefore it admits between itself and God the mean that we have called angelic, bearing the body as the greatest impediment to its destined perfection, just as indeed the lover of wisdom said: “The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul; the earthly dwelling depresses the sense that thinks many things.” Therefore it was altogether necessary for us to believe God rather than to know or understand him, because it is utterly impossible for that super-divine and uncircumscribable majesty to be comprehended by us, who understand nothing without the service of the senses and the discourse of reason.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

But God, existing far above every position, remains subject neither to the senses of mortals nor to reason, as he is read to have said to Moses: “Man shall not see me and live.” Hence also the divine evangelist John says: “No one has ever seen God.” Nor is it any wonder: for since God is the first and everlasting intellect, most pure, most simple, most perfect, immovable, creator, incomprehensible, highest, and far beyond every position, immeasurable and uncircumscribable, he could not be comprehended by the human intellect, which is impure, subject to composition, imperfect, movable, created, comprehensible, lowest, and established under the measure of position.

To that question, however, which seemed to arise from the first, whether God, since he is omnipotent, could have made himself knowable to the human intellect as to the angelic: I say that God can do all things; no one of sound mind has ever denied it. But those things that imply contradiction we say God cannot do, because they are contrary to the order of the wisdom of the immutable one who disposes all things, just as destruction is not doubted to be contrary to the construction of the whole at the same time, and, if I may say so, utterly opposed. For it was neither fitting, nor could it in any way have happened, that God should be comprehended by the human intellect, since if mortal man, under the guidance of nature, comprehended immortal God, certainly he would no longer seem to be called man or mortal, but an angel, and either man would be made comparable to God, or God to man. For so long as the angelic intellect stands between, it does not [unclear].

To the Emperor Maximilian.

The human [intellect] cannot understand God, [unclear] until the death of the flesh, by which the mind, [unclear] natural freedom, will pass out wholly equal to an angel. You now see, I believe, Emperor, that it is manifest that it neither befitted nor was possible that the human intellect should comprehend the divine: the created comprehend the creator, the temporal the eternal, the changeable the unchangeable, the weak the omnipotent, since, as a certain philosopher says, there is either no proportion at all of the finite to the infinite. Therefore it is necessary for mortals to believe God immortal, things which we manifestly can comprehend by no reasoning. Although the order of the whole universe declares that providence is the author of all things, and we understand that nothing produced exists without a beginning except him, nevertheless what God is and how he is the human mind cannot grasp, since, being far above all things that we can understand concerning him, or that any mortal can, he is far outside and above every affirmation, as holy Dionysius says: inasmuch as he is neither soul nor sense, nor has imagination, or opinion, or reason, or understanding; nor is he reason, nor understanding; nor is he spoken, nor understood; nor is he number, nor multitude, nor order, nor magnitude, nor smallness, nor equality, nor likeness, nor unlikeness; nor does he stand, nor is he moved, nor does he act in repose; nor has he power, nor is he power; nor is he light, nor does he live, nor is he life; nor is he substance, nor age, nor [unclear], nor has his spiritual [unclear] been made; nor is he form, nor truth, nor kingdom, nor wisdom, nor one, nor deity, or goodness; nor is he spirit, so far as we ourselves can know; nor is there denomination of son or of father, nor any other thing among those things which has ever been known to us or to another in the world; nor is he anything of those things which are not, nor of those things which are; nor do the things which are know him as he is; nor is there speech of him, nor name, nor knowledge; nor is he darkness, nor light, nor error, nor truth; nor is there any affirmation of him at all, nor removal. For, as the perfect and singular cause of all things is above every affirmation, so the excellence of him, namely of him who, simply absolved from all things, is above all things, is above every removal.

Therefore we say, Dionysius says, that, since as the cause of all things he is above all, he is neither without substance nor without life, nor lacks reason or mind; nor is he body, nor figure, nor form, nor has quality or quantity or death; nor is he in a place, nor is he seen, nor has sensible touch; nor does he sense, nor is he sensible; nor is he subject to rashness or disturbance, stirred by fleshly passions; nor is he weak, subject to sensible accidents; nor is he deprived of light; nor does he admit alteration, or corruption, or division, or flux; nor is he or has he anything else among sensible things. Hence, since he is far above every affirmation, excelling beyond what is supposed, he could not be comprehended by a created being which necessarily uses the senses for understanding, just as the true Peripatetic said: nothing is in our intellect unless it has first been in the senses. Therefore God, who is not subject to the senses of mortals, far exceeds the human intellect; according to affirmative affirmation he truly is altogether in all things; according to negative removal, the nearer he is approached, he is none of all the things that are subject to the knowledge of mortals. Indeed, since he is above all things, he can be none of the things that are subject to him. Therefore beautifully simili-

To Maximilian Caesar.

[unclear] Empedocles gave a likeness, saying: God is a sphere whose center is everywhere, whose circumference is nowhere. Let the human intellect now raise itself as much as it can; and let him who strives to comprehend God comprehend, if he can rightly understand it, the center of this imagined sphere and, at the same time, its circumference ending nowhere. But if he is not equal to understanding this by the proposition of a proper likeness, why does he strive to investigate the essence of God, which exists above every position?

Let it not weary you, most unconquered Caesar, to hear another likeness concerning God from Cusanus, a priest of the Roman Church, cardinal, my fellow Mosellan, a man most learned in those times, who says: God is a straight line of infinite length, which makes a circle. Let us therefore now consider. If the line is straight, how does it make a circle? Or, if it makes a circle, how is it straight? For a circle and a straight line are naturally opposed. Nevertheless, a line of infinite length, since it has neither beginning nor end, necessarily makes a circle, although it is proposed to be imagined not as curved but as straight.

Since, therefore, God is infinite, greatest without quantity, best without quality, all things in all without circumscription, above all things without an excluding position, it was not possible that he should be comprehended by the circumscribable human intellect, which uses the ministry of the senses for understanding, and that what is promised to it when purified, at last in the homeland, should be granted to it while confused and impure on the way. But afterward, when our mind, at last released from the flesh, has escaped clean, simple, pure, perfect, and consummated to the highest center, which is God, having been made equal to the angels, we shall know God perfectly, and all things, just as also Saint Christophilus says to the Corinthians: We now see through a mirror and in an enigma; then face to face.

For this reason we said that the angelic intellect adheres immovably to the beginning given to its nature, because it is pure act and habit, which, since by condition it is naturally simple, cannot be impeded by any commerce of composition. But the human intellect, which has now sufficiently been shown to be potentiality and privation, is impure because of its commerce with its body; yet it is not held back from act forever, but only until, at last released from the flesh, it shall have passed over into the fellowship of likeness with the angels, then for the first time to be admitted to the true knowledge of God.

But if, meanwhile, the affection of love necessary for salvation is joined to present Christian faith and to future divine knowledge, the same everlasting blessedness prepared with the holy angels will be given to the worshippers of God. But if a depraved mind, through too much commerce with its flesh, has scorned the love of God, the intellect, once released from its prison, will indeed escape to the measure of sublime knowledge competent to it by nature, but it will be the more miserable in proportion as, by evil will, it is found to be more like the demons.

Therefore, to conclude, as far as I have been able, the solution of the proposed question, I say that it is not possible for almighty God to be understood perfectly by us so long as we, mortal, are living in the flesh.

To Maximilian Caesar.

On Faith Necessary for Salvation.

The Second Question.

This was the second question of your unconquered Majesty: since only a small part of the world today is subject to the laws of the Christian faith, whether that opinion of very many persons seems admissible without injury to the truth, who think that each person, in the religion which he believes to be true and salutary, as a worshipper of the one God, can be saved outside the Christian faith and without Baptism, provided nothing is known concerning the religion of Christ.

I judged it superfluous to answer this question simply according to the common intention, since I know that today there are many among Christians whom an impious piety, for the salvation of lost men, makes cruel toward God. But because a reason of just consideration moved your most serene Highness to ask these things, not because you do not know what must be held in this Catholic proposition, but so that you might have something with which to set the truth against those who attack it, I shall answer the questions asked as briefly as I can. If anyone could be saved outside the Christian faith, Christ, the Son of almighty God, would seem to have been made man superfluously and without cause. For if there is salvation outside Christ, Christ is not the savior of all. But because it was necessary, according to the Scriptures, that the only-begotten Son of God, for the salvation of the human race, be born as a man in the world, suffer, die, and rise again on the third day, he did not come into this world in vain, nor superfluously, nor without cause. Since this is so, whoever asserts that anyone can be saved outside the faith of Christ shows himself to be not a Christian but an adversary of the faith and a deserter of Christ. For whoever does not believe in Christ, the Son of God, promises himself eternal salvation in vain. For he who is Truth, Jesus Christ, says in the holy Gospel: “He who has not believed will be condemned.” And again: “He who does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.” And again, a little later, he says, adding: “He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.” Saint [Christophilus?] also says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God.”

The solution to the proposed question is now plain to all who truly believe in Christ: because salvation is through him, the Savior of the world, and whoever does not believe in him cannot be saved. Nor is it lawful for a Christian in any way to overstep the boundaries of his religion, so as to presume to correct this question otherwise than Christ taught. But whoever goes beyond this norm of faith by asserting the contrary plainly demonstrates that he does not think rightly concerning Christ, the savior of the faithful. For whoever promises salvation to anyone outside Christ wishes to declare Christ a liar. But we, confirmed by the most sacred ordinances of the Gospel, firmly believe and pronounce without doubt that no one can be saved outside the faith of Christ, however holy or justly he may live, however much he may trust in his paternal or another religion. Christ is salvation; outside the Christian faith no one will be saved. For to what end did Christ, God’s

...and those whom he foreknew would turn aside to evil, he would not bring forth, in so great a multitude, to destruction. For it would seem better not to be than to be badly.

To this question let him answer, if anyone thinks himself God’s counselor. Who am I, that I should expound the cause of the divine will? For all things whatsoever the Lord willed he did in heaven and on earth, and there is no one who can resist his will. Hence a certain wise man says to God: Who will charge it against you if the nations that you made have perished? The Almighty established for things an order of vicissitude, which he will never revoke by any fullness of change. For just as he permits his sun to rise upon the good and the wicked, so also until the end of the age he has caused human beings to be conceived, born, and to grow, both pious and impious. In God there are not the thoughts of human beings, nor does he change his counsel according to time; but since he is unchangeable and [unclear], willing all things together and at once and always, he has from eternity preordained them invariably. God speaks once, as sacred Scripture bears witness, and adds that whatever he wills, he wills immovably, and admits no change. Therefore that human beings should be born good and evil, pious and impious, faithful and faithless, sinners and saints, to be saved and to be damned, God permits by a most just reason, he who assigned this order to all things. Nothing perishes to God, who is Lord of all, and he everywhere holds firm dominion no less over wicked human beings and spirits than over good ones. Christ Jesus, God from God the Father without time, and man from the Virgin in time, appointed mediator of God and human beings, is himself the one through whom we have access to God; he himself is the Savior of all the faithful, concerning whom you think wrongly, who suppose that without the Christian faith anything can...

To Maximilian Caesar.

... rashly concedes that he can be saved. The omnipotence of God has regard to the order of things which he established; according to the inviolable sequence of its rectitude, no one will be saved without faith in Christ, no one who does not believe in the Son of God will be justified. Therefore they are moved by vain and most foolish piety who think that anyone in the whole world and in any sect whatever is to be saved outside the faith of Christ, since this is manifestly contrary to his sentence. Let them hear the Savior himself again saying in the Gospel: No one comes to the Father except through me; for I am the way, the truth, and the life. If no one comes to the Father except through the Son, certainly no one will be saved except through him. Who will save the Jew and the pagan, since no one can be saved except through Christ? But Christ will undoubtedly save only those who in heart, speech, and deed believe in him. He will not save the Jew, not the Saracen, not the pagan, not any other unbeliever, because they do not believe in him, but despise his teaching, scorn the faith, and, blaspheming his holy name, hold it cheap all day long. For he himself said in the Gospel: Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, I also will be ashamed of him before my Father and his holy angels. Tell me now, you who worship Christ and contend that someone can be saved in his own sect, which he thinks true, outside the Christian faith: do you believe the Gospel of Christ to be true or false? If true, why do you think contrary to it? For Christ says: he who does not believe in the Son of God, the wrath of God remains upon him, and he has already been judged and will be condemned. And because no one comes to the Father except through me. But you, led astray by I know not what rashness, press the contrary, saying that a man outside the faith of Christ, trusting in his paternal religion, which he believes to be true and pleasing to God,

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

or living innocently according to the law of nature, and especially since perhaps he has never heard anything at all about the faith of Christ, is to be saved in his confidence. Christ did not say this, but: Whoever has believed in the only-begotten Son of God will be saved; but whoever has not believed will be condemned. He excepted no one, he adds no condition. Since he had come to suffer for all, he had provided for salvation through faith alone. If faith in the Savior is lacking, now no confidence will save the unbeliever. For the holy prelate Augustine said in On Faith to Peter: Hold most firmly, and by no means doubt, that not only all pagans, but also all Jews, heretics, and schismatics who end this present life outside the Catholic Church, will go into the eternal fire prepared for the Devil and his angels. You now perceive where foolish pity drags you, who, measuring God by human laws, so that in all things you may make his only-begotten Son, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, merciful, do not fear to judge him a liar. But Christ is truthful, who says that those not believing in him are to be damned. But we are rash and liars, who trust that anyone can be saved outside his faith. Whoever truly believes in Christ in no way permits anyone at all outside the unity of the Catholic Church of Christians to be said to be saved; whoever says the contrary shows that he is not a true and good Christian. For this is the immovable sentence of Catholic tradition, which the Lord Jesus himself defined in the holy Gospel: namely, that no one is to be saved outside his faith, which he himself established, taught, and confirmed with his own blood. Therefore whoever [unclear] a man to be saved …who has affirmed that a man in any sect outside the faith of Jesus Christ, or has believed it in his heart, is not a good Christian, but rather an apostate and a disciple of Antichrist; and unless he comes to his senses, let him know that he will be tormented forever in the lower world with him. For he is Antichrist, not a Christian, who says that one who does not believe in the Lord Jesus is to be saved without the Savior. Therefore, most wise Caesar, let no one appear in the sight of Your Majesty, let no one perceive you as adhering to him, who thinks that men outside the faith of Jesus Christ are to be saved. For everyone who has believed that anyone is to be saved outside the faith of Christ has denied both Christ and his Gospel. But that we say that all who are not Christians are to be condemned is an indication not of cruelty but of truthful piety. For it is better to believe firmly in the truth than falsely to agree with a man. That all Jews, pagans, gentiles, Saracens, schismatics, heretics, and unbelievers are without doubt to be condemned with the demons is attested by the Church of the saints, which took and confirmed this judgment from nowhere other than from the words of Christ. For thus he said: He who believes in the Son has eternal life; by this are designated Christians who are good in faith and work. But he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. Here are denoted all Jews, pagans, Saracens, gentiles, and whoever do not believe in our Lord Jesus Christ. Concerning schismatics and heretics, however, the judgment of Christ is clear, when he says in the Gospel: Whoever refuses to hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican. Heathens are gentiles, and publicans are manifest and public sinners; concerning their condemnation, most certain among the saints, the Church does not doubt. For who among Christians would have doubted that gentiles and enormous sinners, manifest and public, are to be condemned? Why then do schismatics

16 Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions

and heretics, all of whom despise the Church of the saints, being most rightly said on account of their offenses to be like the gentiles and publicans who are to be condemned for their crimes, justly undergo punishments of eternal damnation equal with them? Behold, those whom the just sentence of Christ the Savior condemned, the foolish compassion of men, not to say impious cruelty, presumes are to be saved. They desire to be merciful toward lost men; they do not fear to show themselves cruel toward God, whom he through justice assigned to death: these men, with the worst presumption, by recalling them assert that they are to be brought to life. It is neither good nor useful for a Christian, whether seriously or in jest, to contradict Christ; he is impious, not a Christian, whoever says that unbelievers are to be saved. When Adam, the first man, perished, we all sinned; the wrath of God remained upon the whole human race from the beginning of the world until Christ. Christ came, born of a virgin, who, God and man, innocent of sin, voluntarily underwent the death of the cross; having been made mediator between God and man, he removed the wrath due to original guilt from those who believe in him. For thus he says: He who believes in the only-begotten Son of God has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. Indeed, without faith in Jesus Christ no one will be saved, however much he may seem to live justly and holily in his own religion. For almighty God can save a believer without material baptism, but he cannot make a denier saved without faith. Let no one be saved unwillingly, because no one believes except willingly; for God knows who are his, since those who believe in the Son he has through repentance, but unbelievers he condemns through the equity of justice.

Hence, when access was barred, a new question struck the mind: what

To Maximilian Caesar.

what is to be thought concerning the infants and the simple-minded of unbelieving pagans and Jews. To this one must reply: just as the infants of Christians, baptized in the faith of their parents, are saved, so the children of all unbelievers, not baptized, will be damned in the unbelief of their parents. The judgment concerning the simple-minded of either religion is similar: just as we believe without doubt that baptized simple-minded Christians are to be saved, so we say without doubt that those of unbelievers are to be damned.

Again it is asked here what is to be held in Catholic belief concerning those people who inhabit the islands newly discovered in the great sea, of which no mention is made among the ancient cosmographers, and who, as we have been informed, have never heard anything at all of the Christian religion. A brief answer, conformable in all respects to what has been set forth, is given: since Truth exempts no unbeliever at all from damnation, neither [unclear] of the islands, nor one contiguous to our world, nor anyone else dwelling either near or far, but has concluded all without distinction, without defining persons, saying: “He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned”; “the wrath of God remains upon him.” Who removes the wrath of God from man, except our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the mediator of God and men? By what means, except through faith formed in him, who, though innocent, tasted death? Since, therefore, without faith no one can [attain?] salvation, those who are known not to have the piety of faith in him [unclear]. Accordingly we must necessarily say that all are to be damned who do not believe in the Son of God, whether they have heard of him or are wholly ignorant of him.

One thing, however, we grant: that if there were any among those who are ignorant of Christ who lived well according to the law of nature, invoking the one God, even if they sometimes sinned, provided they had done penance before death, they were damned, or are to be damned, less gravely than those who either hear of Christ and despise him, or in either case have lived wickedly and foully. For God is just; he does injury to no one, but renders to each according to his works. Yet the wrath of God remains upon everyone who does not believe in his only-begotten Son, on account of the original sin of the first man, from which no one is justified except through faith and baptism of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

If original sin alone is present in a person, as in little children, unless it is removed through Christ, it condemns the one who has it only to the punishment of loss, whereby, namely, he is barred forever from the vision of God and the enjoyment of the blessedness of the saints. But an adult who sins mortally will be punished after death with a twofold punishment, namely of loss and of sense, so that he both does not see God and, feeling the pains of Gehenna without end, never escapes. Jews, Saracens, and all the rest who, hearing the faith of Christ, despise it are without doubt damned to the punishment both of loss and of sense, whether otherwise they live innocently according to the law of nature or the contrary. But among those who have never heard of Christ, if any should live innocent according to the law of nature up to death, I do not think that they have furnished cause for being said or believed to be damned to the punishment of sense, although they are deprived forever of the vision of God, which theologians have called the punishment of loss; for no one will behold the face of God the Father almighty unless he has been reborn through faith in Christ.

Now let us conclude with a judgment against those who, when we assert these things in Catholic fashion according to Christ’s doctrine, object with weighty consideration.

that almighty God, since he is supremely good, wished to create so many thousands of human beings whom from eternity he foreknew were to be damned. For if a comparison is made of Christians with unbelievers, scarcely a twentieth part of the people of the whole world today believes in our Lord Jesus Christ. The immense curiosity of this question has often greatly troubled [unclear]; if faith in Christ were firm in them, and devotion fervent in love, they would not seek such [unclear] difficult matters. For what man of such learning or sanctity is found among mortals that, apart from God himself, he could disclose to us the cause of the divine will? For the cause of the will of God is incomprehensible, since he himself is the cause of his own most righteous will. The eternal order is inviolable; as I said in the preceding matter, God does injury to no one. Was it not the case that, when God judged the flood of the whole world upon the earth, only eight persons were saved in the ark, while all the rest perished in the inundation of waters? The cause of their perishing was sin. But that they were created had no other cause than the uncircumscribable goodness of God. That few are saved while many perish was prefigured by the mystery of Noah’s ark, the sacrament of the Christian faith. For just as all outside Noah’s ark perished in the flood, so now all who are outside the unity of the Catholic Church of Christians will without doubt perish eternally in their sins, Jews as well as pagans, heretics together with schismatics. The justice of God damns those whom his goodness created; but mercy saves those whom grace has confirmed. For, as the holy Apostle says, it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy, since he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. If we weigh human freedom of will rightly in this way, we shall know the will of God to be just.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions

On the Miracles of Unbelievers

Third Question

[unclear]

The third question of your most serene Majesty was: if no one is saved outside the faith, whence come miracles among unbelievers? For we have learned from the reports of many that astonishing things occur even among unbelievers.

The solution of this question, as it seems to me, will not be difficult if we apply both faith in the Scriptures and the necessary consideration of the natural powers of the soul. Now a miracle is a new and unusual occurrence, which, because of [unclear], happens and draws people into wonder. Hence good Christians work miracles in one way, the wicked in another, and unbelievers in another. Good Christians indeed work miracles through public justice, but the wicked through signs of public justice; unbelievers, however, through private contracts with demons, that is, whether implicit or explicit. Concerning the good, indeed, the Lord said in the holy Gospel: “These signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it shall not harm them; they shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall be well.” But concerning wicked Christians who work miracles in the name of Jesus Christ, it is written thus in the Gospel:

To Maximilian Caesar.

We read in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day, Lord, Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name, and in your name do many mighty works? And then I shall declare to them: I never knew you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity.” But outside the Church of God, where the name of our Lord Jesus Christ is not invoked, if any marvels occur beyond the usual course of nature or of human art, no good Christian doubts that they are done by the cooperation of demons. And works of this kind your Imperial Serenity judges, by discernment of their power, should rather be called marvels than miracles. Nor does this judgment of truth depart from reason, insofar as there should be a necessary distinction between prodigies of light and of darkness. I find four agents of marvels, but I recognize principally one alone, God, who performs true miracles, as the cause of all good things.

Therefore the first and greatest agent of all marvelous things is God, who, filling the whole world with signs, miracles, and powers, has illumined it; with him none of the others is to be compared. He created heaven and earth, the sea and all things that are in them; he alone is omnipotent, just, holy and upright, good, incomprehensible, greatest, glorious, immense and everlasting. All other things are beneath him. For whatever can happen marvelously in this world is certainly less than the whole world itself, which he was able to create from nothing. Likewise every miracle that can be performed through a human being is less than the human being himself, since God, creator of all things, formed him in the beginning to his greatness and likeness. And although the miracles of God among visible natures have, through the constancy with which mortals see them, now almost become cheapened, nevertheless, if we examine them wisely, then they will appear greater and rarer than all things that are unusual.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

But the manner of performing miracles in God is the immutable will of God, who, since he is omnipotent, does all things whatsoever he has willed in heaven and on earth. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. The will of God is ordered and everlasting; therefore his miracles are incomparably greater than the rest. For greater than all the miracles of this world is that we behold the whole universe, and whatever is contained in it, created by the will of God. The immutable divine will, persisting, works all things, since it lacks both beginning and end; but whatever God wills, he always wills, because, since willing and being able are the same in him, it does not belong to the immutable to labor. Hence all the universal miracles that the maker of all things performs he has offered for both good and evil people to behold. And after the general miracles, which have now grown common by use among mortals, he has also displayed, in almost individual creatures, infinite things specially worthy of wonder.

The second agent of miracles is the good angel, who very often works marvels for mortals both by natural power and by divine authority. For those most blessed spirits are sent by divine ordinance in ministry to the faithful, and they provide to both good and evil people those things that are benefits of nature. But to those alone who believe in God and in our Lord Jesus Christ they administer the gift of saving grace. Hence there is no doubt that those miracles which are done in the Church of the saints by invocation of the divine name are exhibited by their ministry and cooperation; but the marvels of the unbelievers, if any are either done today or are read to have been done formerly, are either fabricated or falsely claimed, or are prepared by the mockery of demons. For it cannot happen that mini-

by the ministry of good angels any unbelievers perform miracles: for where Christ Jesus, the Son of God, is not believed in, no signs of grace are displayed through good spirits to impious and reprobate men. Indeed, since they are obstinate in the error of false religion, if in their own estimation they have obtained anything miraculous, there is no doubt whatever that it is done through the ministry of demons. For since they are wholly unlike the good angels, they obtain no familiarity with them. For no despiser of the Christian faith can please God; but whoever is proved displeasing to almighty God is without doubt deprived of the familiarity of the holy angels. Yet by this we do not withdraw from anyone every good spirit assigned to him, by whose ministry, even if he is unbelieving toward the Son of God, he may receive the benefits of nature, although he does not attain to the gifts of grace. But upon those who believe in our Lord Christ they confer not only the benefits of nature, but also minister the gifts of grace. It is therefore manifest that, if any miracles are done among unbelievers, they cannot be done by the gift of God or by the ministry of the holy angels, since all who are placed outside the unity of the Church cannot work signs by public justice when they are impious. For God, as has been said, does not remove his original wrath from man except through faith in Jesus Christ; but everyone who is unbelieving toward the Son of God will not see eternal life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. Therefore everyone upon whom the wrath of God remains will not be able to please God; and so the wonders that are done at his prayers should be believed to be performed not by the power of God nor by the ministry of angels, but rather by the intervention of demons. The third worker of wonders is the devil, who, like an ape, tries to imitate whatever he sees, and deceives the minds of men, especially unbelievers, with various illusions,

24 Joh. Trithemius, Eight Questions

and seduces those who believe him by a certain likeness of miracles. For I do not judge it difficult for demons to be able to delude the senses of men, since it is agreed that by nature they were created more subtle than all mortals. But they cannot know the thoughts of mortals except by a certain conjecture, since of course by nature we make our inward matters manifest by certain signs. Demons foretell future things, and sometimes speak the truth, sometimes are deceived in conjecturing and deceive. From the beginning of the world they have known certain signs antecedent to events; by experience and use of these they sometimes foretell truly what is to come. And when they have seen signs known to them that precede an event, they immediately conjecture what is in a man’s thought; yet very often they deceive, because they themselves are deceived. For when they are asked about some matter which they do not know, as, for example, whether a messenger sent far away is going to return soon, or on what day, they immediately, in the blink of an eye, reach the place where they know him to be. When they have seen that he has already begun the journey to return, they carefully count the days, and, having suddenly returned to the one who asked, confidently affirm that the absent man will come on a fixed day. But if he has delayed on the road or has turned aside elsewhere, then certainly the demons, already deceived in their judgment, must be mistaken. They gladly insert themselves into prophecies, and are ready enough to foretell future things to men for the sake of the honor and esteem which they most greatly desire to have, as being worthy of admiration. They seek divine honors, and greatly long to be feared by mortals. Just as boys hiding in a hidden place, or running about masked, suddenly bursting out from their hiding places, strike with unexpected terror their companions who suspect nothing hidden, and again, lest they be recognized

To Maximilian Caesar.

[unclear] they hide themselves again; and when they observe the ignorant to be terrified, they boast as though they seemed to have obtained from this some great honor. Demons of this kind, indeed, more fastened to the earth and those who move about among human beings, are very restless; the ancients called them [Bacuaeos?]. They terrify people at night, and seek nothing more from mortals than the esteem of divinity. Hence, in the presence of those with whom they are permitted to be by reason of likeness, they sometimes perform various mockeries, and, as chance allows, present themselves in minds as terrifying. As often as they can, they gladly assume the likeness of a human body, but they do not always find suitable material of air with which to be clothed; for this reason they rather often appear monstrous and horrible, because they have not had suitable [unclear] or vapors for the perfection of the appearance desired. Moreover, the more they are fastened to earthly dwellings, the more by chance they have become dull with respect to the material of their making. Hence, because of the ignorance which they contracted through disobedience, the predictions of demons are frequently false, although by divine permission they are sometimes even verified. For, as that most holy John Chrysostom says, it has been granted to the devil sometimes to speak truth, so that he may commend his lie by a rare truth. For if he never spoke truth, he could deceive no one, and his seduction would by no means suffice for tempting. It is therefore no wonder if demons sometimes seem to foretell true things to unbelieving people, since they once were able to present prophecies in the idols of the gentiles. Nor is it any wonder if they sometimes provide care to the sick, since they know the natures of diseases, and can remove diseases which they had previously brought on, or withdraw for a time from the senses those which chance has inflicted.

But almighty God, by the right of his sovereign majesty, uses the ministry of all beings, even demons, both for the testing of the faithful and for the punishment of the impious. Since they are perverse in affection, obstinate in their rebellion, and proud, they especially desire divine estimation and honors; and for that reason they gladly come to the invocations of unbelievers, which they are accustomed to pour forth to their gods, as though they themselves were gods. Among unbelievers they sometimes seem to raise the dead back to life, and they show marvelous things to curious people, so that by what are like miracles they render them, confirmed in their former error, stubborn against the Lord. Yet they do not truly raise the dead, but deceive human senses in various ways, since either they themselves enter the corpses of the dead and carry them around there for a time as though alive, or, after those bodies have been removed to a more distant place, they present to the spectators for viewing some image in the semblance of the dead person’s life. Just as the experience of certain people has informed us, we believe it evident that demons can show in a certain false likeness all the things whatever that the saints do as miracles in truth. All the miracles of demons are either phantasms or things done by a certain natural skill. For if people experienced in the more hidden mysteries of nature, by some combination of matter concealed from others, bring forth unusual and marvelous effects into form, just as [unclear] from the dew of heaven, bees from the flesh of [unclear], serpents from certain roots of herbs, and many other things of this kind, if I do not wish to mention greater ones, as proof in many cases has made you experienced, who would deny that demons, of a subtler nature and greater experience, can work naturally more marvelous things which are manifest to no human beings?

To Maximilian Caesar.

The fourth worker of miracles, however, is man, who works marvelous things in four ways, which to those who know neither their cause nor their manner do not seem human.

And first, by invocation of the divine name, when, in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the merit of accepted holiness is joined with it. In this way the holy apostles and their imitators, by the power of God and at the same time by the merit of holiness in the unity of faith, performed miracles. But unbelievers cannot perform miracles in this way, because they do not walk the necessary path of faith unto salvation. For although many of them believe in one Lord, yet because they refuse to believe in the mediator between God and men, they have gone very far away from God’s mercy. But, as the holy Gospel promises, all things are possible to those who believe in God and our Lord Jesus Christ: namely, to those who adorn right faith also with holy works. For just as without faith it is impossible to please God, so also faith without works is dead. Almighty God would grant us all things that we ask in the faith of Christ, if we did all things according to the faith as we ought. Believe firmly and work faithfully, and you will always obtain all things.

Secondly, man performs miracles by likeness to angelic purity. For the purer our mind, confirmed in the faith of Jesus Christ through love, has become, the more, having been made like the holy angels, it attains their greater familiarity. For whoever has altogether attained the familiarity of the holy angels, when he wishes, by God’s bounty, he will shine forth in miracles. For the holy angels reveal to pure men, fervent in the love of God, secrets hidden from others, and by the Creator’s command they make many things manifest to him. For the Lord is near to those who call upon him in truth. The Lord will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayers and save them. For whoever has been united with Christ through grace is refreshed by the frequent visitation of angels, and often, when necessity demands it, is illumined by their ministry, and often also by their powers. Hence it is that even those weighed down by various illnesses betake themselves to the intercessions of the saints and, recalling the Lord’s promises to a friend, obtain by the merits of others what they cannot by their own; their holy devotion in the faith of Christ receives health from the Lord, when, aided both by the purity of its own conscience and supported by the merit of another’s holiness, it rises not rashly into certain hope.

In the Church of God, however, miracles are performed by divine power with a threefold consideration or means. For sometimes almighty God works a miracle by the ministry of angels, solely through the merits of the one working it, as Saint Martin healed a blind man and a lame man against their will. Sometimes miracles are performed through the merit of the sufferers alone, as we read that many were cured by bad Christians, because the sick believed them to be excellent in the faith. Thirdly, there is no doubt that healings of this kind are performed through the merit of both, namely of the sufferer and the worker together, as Christ says to someone in the holy Gospel: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes.” For faith is required for a miracle to such an extent that our Lord Jesus Christ, coming into his own country, wondered that he could not do any mighty work there because of their unbelief. But none of these things is done among unbelievers, where neither holiness is found in the worker nor orthodox faith in the sufferer.

Thirdly, therefore, man performed miracles by means of coope—

by the cooperation of diabolical depravity. And this can happen in three ways: namely by the manifest invocation of demons, by implication, and by supposition.

By manifest invocation necromancers, and little women whom we commonly call witches, do wondrous things; they, corrupted by a likeness of will, have passed into fellowship with demons. For just as in the Church of God the sacraments are signs of the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit, so in the school of demons certain characters, invocations, and methods are the marks of a depraved man and a malignant spirit. Hence, when witches display the signs of demons, the malignant spirits invoked are accustomed willingly to come to them and to exhibit horrible and at the same time wondrous acts of witchcraft.

But witches and necromancers produce wondrous effects by the invocation of demons in different ways. Witches are subjected to demons by a certain kind of profession; by their service they disturb the air, raise storms, devastate crops, make men and beasts ill, carry on foul commerce with demons in most filthy pleasure, and by destructive charms call back from below into sight whomever they have wished. Their deeds are not to be called miracles, but rather witchcrafts, deservedly to be punished with the ultimate penalty.

Necromancers, however, not by manifest profession but by an implicit condition, promise to compel demons to appear visibly in a circle by the display of characters, and also by sacrifices, fumigations, and vows. Their crimes are infinite, since it is manifest that all enter into fellowship with demons, either implicitly or explicitly. Although not all necromancers are equal either in art or in practice, nevertheless all agree in their own destruction through damnable curiosity, by which, with the aid of demons, they desire to attain what they cannot discover by nature. All their works and books are full of superstitions and impiety, and for that reason must be driven far from the borders of believers.

There is a great multitude of enchanters and necromancers in the East, who by their illusions miserably deceive the human race, and have turned away almost all of greater and lesser Asia from the faith of Christ. Illusions can occur in three ways: by the service of demons, by the operation of nature, and by the deception of human art. No true Christian will doubt that the miracles of those unbelievers occur in that way, where the determined root of the worker is placed. But today there are very many among Christians who are devoted to the works of demons: enchanters, witches, reprobates in matters of faith, who deceive many by excessive curiosity and by their arts promise impossibilities.

By implication of demons, moreover, wondrous things sometimes happen: namely whenever a man not sufficiently rightly confirmed in the faith does or wishes something otherwise than befits a Christian, even if he believes it to be no sin. Since this ought not to happen, nevertheless the Devil, intruding himself, very often supplies the desired effect. Such is that which the [unclear] commonly use: on the holy day of Parasceve, during the office, they make a ring of whatever metal, which they thereafter always wear on the ring finger. These things are utterly vain and have no root of truth at all. Yet I have seen certain persons cured by the same [unclear]

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions

[unclear] by [unclear] herbs [unclear] [unclear] [unclear] I saw, [unclear] effects [unclear] [unclear] [unclear] figures, [unclear] often [unclear] deserved [unclear] rather [unclear] [unclear] [unclear] mortal [unclear] [unclear] [unclear] whatever [unclear] [unclear] holy [unclear] Christ [unclear] [unclear] variously [unclear] impulse [unclear] [unclear] [unclear] [unclear] all [unclear] faithless [unclear] of whom

To Emperor Maximilian

I cannot deny that [they were freed?] from a spasm. Likewise, I know that someone opened [locks?] by words and very powerful herbs; this I think was done neither by the power of God nor by the force of the things applied. I could bring forward countless similar things that I have seen and heard, whose effects, if they are manifest, are surely nothing other than certain miracles of demons. For some men, excessively curious, stubbornly placing faith and trust in characters, slips of paper, rings, figures, necklaces, and unknown words, often obtain astonishing effects; these, we do not at all doubt, the devil has supplied, not by merit of holiness nor granted by God’s mercy, but rather through treacherous credulity. For demons, having the greatest envy of the human race, readily come to meet the vain operations of the impious, in order to destroy the souls of mortals. What else are characters and interpretations of hidden names than certain foods and drinks of demons? Whoever places faith in characters promising marvelous effects has implicitly denied both the faith of Christ and the Church of the saints. Alas, how many Christians today, how many clerics, how many priests, to spare greater men, use many and various superstitions in their daily actions, by which they follow the entangled passions of demons, to the disgrace of the Christian faith and to their own condemnation. And because these evils have now multiplied too greatly among Christians, the Almighty has withdrawn his hand and handed them over into the power of destroyers, so that they may feel as exactors of punishments those whom, by imitation, they will stubbornly have served, not the living and true God, but vain superstitions.

3: The Eight Questions of Johannes Trithemius

By the substitution of demons, moreover, we know plainly, if we inquire more diligently into the truth, that astonishing things are done. For the Jews, Saracens, pagans, or gentiles, who do not believe in God our Lord Jesus Christ, if they perform any miracles, we believe that these are done not by the power of God, not by the ministry of angels, not by merit of holiness, but by the substitution of demons. For whenever they invoke almighty God, in whose only-begotten Son they do not believe, for mercy in regard to some marvelous effect, then the devil, coming in, who is not false to sinners, and because the Most High does not hear unbelieving sinners, in order that they may persist in errors, secretly applies himself in place of the God invoked and, if he can, the Lord permitting, grants to [their] prayers what is requested. The devil uses this substitution the more freely, the less he is hindered by the faith of Christ and the sacraments of the Church. For the wrath of God remains upon all unbelievers who do not believe in his only-begotten Son, and [he] was in the power of the devil. And therefore he enters, for those invoking him, in the place of God. Hence, blinded in their errors, while the innocent God, in whose Son they do not believe, fails to hear those remaining in wrath, the devil comes as a false worker of miracles. Therefore those who scorn believing the true miracles of God believe the deceits of the devil. They receive from demons false miracles suited to their errors, those who, by believing, have not chosen to follow the truth, that is, Christ. There have been many among the unbelievers who, worshiping the one God, creator of all things, do not adore idols and firmly believe that they will be saved in their own faith. But because they fail to believe the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, the wrath of God remains upon them; and in their follies they vanish away, thinking that God is near, in whom they do not rightly believe; [they are] subjected to the demon.

To Maximilian Caesar.

[unclear], in whose false miracles, when they place faith, they are confirmed by falsehood in their errors. It should not displease us, O Caesar, to introduce an analogy for this matter. There was a certain swineherd who had enclosed in his staff a little slip containing the name of the holy martyr Blasius; he ascribed so much trust to it that, when the staff was fixed in the ground in the midst of the herd, he believed every wolf was kept from coming near. When this foolish confidence had at last been strengthened by long experience, the man went safely wherever he wished, leaving the pigs in the wood without danger, since no wolf now had any access. It happened that one passing by saw this in the shepherd’s absence; and, observing that demons were keeping guard over the herd, he said to one of them: “What are you doing here, wretch?” He answered: “I am guarding these pigs.” But the other said: “Who entrusted you with the care of the pigs?” Again he answered: “The shepherd’s foolish confidence. For, thinking a certain slip enclosed in a staff to be of great power, by which through the merits of some Blasius wolves are kept from the gates, he has sinned against his own law and follows our vanities. But since the one invoked does not appear, I, lest the man lose his confidence, guard his pigs, and willingly put myself in the place of Blasius.” Thus, he says, mortals trouble us with vain conjurations, so that, unless we wish to lose all esteem and honor for ourselves among them, it often becomes necessary for us to answer their foolish invocations. By the likeness of this event demons deceive wretched unbelievers: the miracles which they ask of God in prayer they very often obtain through the substitution of malignant spirits. For in those things which concern either the worship or the honor of God, demons readily insert themselves; since they cannot obtain open honors, they plainly take delight in hidden ones.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

At the same time it must be noted that, from the beginning of the world, miracles have never been lacking to any religion or sect of principal excellence, although not all have been done from one principle. For whatever miracles have been done in the true religion have been done from no other source than from God. The law of nature had its miracles; the written law had them; grace now has them likewise. Almighty God, who gave religion, himself also works miracles. But in false religions, where truth is not worshiped, if any miracles are done, not God but the devil works them. For since God is truth, he did not institute false religions, and therefore he has never adorned a lie with his miracles. Muhammad, who was full of an evil demon and instituted a false religion, adorned it with false miracles not from God, but by the cooperation of demons. For the demon who gave the cause of error could also, when the occasion had been accepted, display a false miracle to the deceived. Hence, if miracles had been wholly lacking to Muhammad when he was persuading a rude people of a new religion, perhaps no one would have given him credence. For he too showed the peoples certain marvels, both by subtlety of intellect and by the cooperation of the devil, so that he might seem to have confirmed a new doctrine with new miracles as well. Miracles were not lacking even to the pagan idolaters, if we do not deny credence to the histories. The Jews, however, before the incarnation of the Son of God, receiving his law through Moses, were frequently illumined by divine miracles. But after the Lord’s resurrection, when the Mosaic law had been emptied of force, those who do not believe in the only-begotten Son of God remain under the wrath of his indignation, and all miracles of truth have ceased among them. Hence, if today they do any marvelous things, they are works of demons and manifest indications of error. For demons labor especially with zeal to

To Maximilian Caesar.

those men whom they have once made to wander from the way of truth, which is Christ, they make, by the continuance of fraud, obstinate in error even to death. For indeed, when God for just reason withdraws his grace from unbelievers, their deceiver, the malignant spirit, approaches unrecognized; and, seeing that salvation is far away, he seduces the minds of the ignorant by false miracles, as though the Lord were near. Therefore whatever miracles belong to unbelievers are works of demons. For just as outside the unity of the Christian faith there is no salvation for mortals, so without Christ the most holy power of wonders is not granted. For now demons, lurking in ambush, long since conquered and confounded by the trophy of Christ, fear to appear openly as they did before the incarnation of the Lord, and therefore among unbelievers they falsely present themselves as good spirits.

There are also those who add a fourth to the three modes set down above, saying that the mind or spirit of the man himself can naturally do wondrous things, provided it knows how to recall itself from everything adventitious into itself, above the senses, into unity. For those who ascribe such things to nature promise that it can do wonders, foretell the future, disclose the secrets of men, remove diseases, and suddenly change a man’s counsels. But this mode of miracles cannot be simply natural, certain, common, and infallible; for if it is true, something I have not experienced, it is necessary that some external power also come in and that either a good angel or an evil spirit in part occupy the one thinking. But if no external powers intermingle, the one prophesying must form his beginning either from conjectures or from a bold presumption of speaking, and pronounce a judgment sometimes true, sometimes false. For indeed, as long as the spirit dwells in the body, by its nature it naturally understands nothing without the service of the senses.

The Eight Questions of Johannes Trithemius.

Hence I would not altogether resist, if they grant that our confused and crude understanding is aided by a like service. For we see in the case of those who very often, through the desire of inward love for Jesus, pass in contemplation beyond the measure of the flesh, that they are lifted upward from the earth into the air; and we think that they overcome the bodily weight not merely by their own keenness of mind, but no less by divine power. Therefore the three aforementioned principles of opinion, unknown to many, satisfy, in my judgment, few, as the mind is placed in the body. I speak of a thing experienced. When as a young man I was pursuing the studies of letters, four of us were sleeping in one bed on a certain night. One of my own age rose from my side and, asleep as he was accustomed to be in dreams, with eyes closed and with the moon on its fifteenth day shining in, walked about as if awake; he climbed walls and surpassed a squirrel in his agility. While asleep he also crossed over the bed a second and a third time; he trod on all of us with his feet, and we felt his weight no more than if a tiny mouse had touched us. Wherever his sleeping body moved, suddenly all the fastenings of doors opened of themselves. He very swiftly penetrated the higher buildings of the house and clung to the roofs in the manner of a sparrow. I speak of things seen, not heard by vague report. These seem to be functions of the soul, not of the body; the soul uses its natural power, so to speak, almost freely, when, the senses of the flesh being bound, it wanders outside the dwelling of the body. But since the matter does not in every respect suit the proposed question, concerning the causes of these wonders to another

[unclear]

To Emperor Maximilian.

But let us defer the discussion to another time. For we do not believe that these things are wonders to wise men, who have understood very well the power and nobility of the human mind, since, hindered only by the interposition of the body, it is in some respect reckoned equal to the angels. Finally, I pass over the various modes and kinds of fascinations, by which a frenzied person produces very wondrous effects upon external things. The very strong imagination of a confident person can also do much toward producing wonderful effects, whether upon a true object or upon one merely supposed.

Therefore, since there are so many kinds and modes of working wonders, it is no wonder if Jews, Saracens, pagans, gentiles, and all other unbelievers established outside the faith of Christ, who cannot perform miracles through public justice, enact wonders either by the support of demons or by artful industry. Nor does it escape me that, by the same reasoning, the miracles of the saints are attacked by the impious, as if they were not done by the power of the Creator, but rather by the entanglement or substitution of the devil. Whoever truly believes that the Christian faith alone is true does not doubt that the miracles of all unbelievers have been accomplished by the cooperation of demons. But if anyone rashly and stubbornly thinks the contrary, he shows himself to be an unbeliever, not a Christian.

On Sacred Scripture.

Question Four.

The fourth question of your Most Serene Majesty was this: why almighty God did not give Holy Scripture, containing the mysteries of our faith, of both the New and the Old Testament, as open and manifest, uniform in all things, and plainly sufficient for all things, but rather as wrapped up and, in many places, full of riddles. For many things necessary for the perfection of faith are not found sufficiently expressed in the divine Scriptures.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

To this question of your Most Sacred Majesty it seems that one must answer: every Scripture divinely inspired is a perfect work of divinity, ordered and preordained before all time, written in time in no other way than God willed, who inspired men that it should be written. For all the works of God are perfect. And therefore, since the Scripture of which we speak is the work of God, it is necessary to confess that it is perfect in all things. For God, the supreme judge, whose works are all perfect, gave to his Scriptures the order he willed and the one he willed, and without doubt infused into those receiving them how they should write. For almighty God bestowed such authority and majesty upon Sacred Scripture that, in comparison with it, all the words of this world fail, since divine things cannot properly be comprehended in human speech. Therefore divine Scripture, which on the surface of its words appears confused to the ignorant, seems manifest to those who know it, because unless it is read in that spirit by which it is believed to have been infused into men, one by no means arrives at its understanding. The learned man who burns with the embrace of the flesh and with vain desires reads it in one way, and the understanding man, whom the love of God truly inflames after he has been stripped of pleasures, reads it in another. Hence it is no wonder if men wise according to the flesh do not understand the divine Scriptures, who, blinded by the pleasures of the flesh, the sweetness of the Spirit of God [unclear].

To Maximilian Caesar.

[unclear] they have never perceived. Just as, if you show to a boy learning the first elements of letters any written volume whose character is unlike that in his own little book, when he cannot read the writing he will at once cry out that it is bad and not properly formed. In the same way, men who approach the reading of the divine Scriptures, wise only in a fleshly manner, and who do not grasp those things that are of the divine Spirit, burdened by vices and rashness, when they ought to have blamed their own ignorance and unworthiness, reproach as holy the Scriptures which they do not understand. For it is not lawful for everyone everywhere to interpret the divine Scriptures, lest the beast, touching the mountain, be overwhelmed with stones.

Many now arise in a reversed order, who have spent the whole time of their life on humane letters; having become older men, they wrongly interpret the divine Scriptures, which they have never learned, and do not explain them but confuse them, examining them according to their own sense. Hence all who do not understand the sacred Scriptures by that Spirit by which they were breathed into those who wrote them have over their hearts the veil of ignorance and rashness, spread out after the manner of the Jews; from there they very often drink the poison of destructive error, from which those who approach humbly in the Spirit of God have received the cup of salvation.

For heavenly doctrine is not contained in the words of the Scriptures, but in their meaning; not on the surface of the words, but in the understanding; not in the leaves of ornate speech, but in the hidden place of mystical inspiration. Hence the divine Pope Gregory says: Sacred Scripture far surpasses all the sciences of this world in the manner of its speech, since in one and the same discourse, while it recounts the text, it reveals a hidden mystery; just as it refreshes the simple on the surface, so it exercises the wise with mystery. For it has in public that from which it may nourish little ones; it preserves in secret that by which it may suspend the minds of the lofty in wonder at its sweetness, like a certain marvelous river in which both the simple little lamb may walk and the great elephant may swim.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

And St. Augustine says on Genesis: Divine Scripture speaks in such a way that by its height it mocks the proud, by its depth it terrifies the attentive, by its strength it feeds the great, and by its affability it nourishes little ones. For the authority of sacred Scripture is greater than all the perspicacity of human talent. Therefore, in order that one may come to their true understanding, above all the mind must be cleansed of every carnal affection, and the aid of divine goodness must be diligently implored with humility, so that by his Spirit he may illumine the understanding of the learner.

For all necks of powers must be subjected to the authority of the divine Scriptures. And, as the divine Jerome says, one must never flatter a man in such a way that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected; in the whole of both Testaments it is true in its narration of deeds, right in its admonitions, certain in its promises, and terrifyingly to be feared in its threats. Therefore it has not been given to all to be able to penetrate the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, but it is permitted in some measure only to those in whom love makes study continuous, and to whose purified minds the Spirit of God grants true understanding.

But whoever is foul with the darkness of vices, whoever walks with a swollen mind, proud; whoever doubts the truth of the Scriptures of God, whether in part or in whole, let him never trust that he can attain to their understanding. For the authority of Scripture itself says that unless you have believed, you will not understand. The slowness of our talent is ours, and so too the impurity of our desire, whenever we do not rightly understand the divine Scriptures, namely when the veil of pernicious occupation

To Maximilian Caesar.

... remains spread over our hearts, which does not permit us to arrive at true understanding. Hence it happens that we do not understand the sense which the Holy Spirit has poured into the divine Scriptures, but, seizing the bare words of the writers, we twist them into another sense. Indeed, if our minds were purged of carnal vices, if through the continual pursuit of sobriety the intellect were stirred up in the Scriptures, if belief and reverence were applied as their dignity requires, every student would understand more clearly than light that in the sacred readings there is nothing confused, nothing misshapen, nothing unsuitable, nothing absurd, or inserted without the most just reason. For all the passages of divine Scripture are full of mysteries; and whenever anything in them seems to have been set down obscurely, this has been done by divine providence, so that the studious mind may have the necessary exercise of piety, and the faith of the simple may not lose the place of due reverence. Therefore not by chance, but by eternal providence, he willed the holy Scriptures to be obscure in many places, so that it might abound in as many mysteries as senses in which, by the inspiration of the Spirit of God, it is explained in Catholic fashion by the doctors. For, as holy Augustine says, the obscurity of divine Scripture is useful and very profitable, because it begets many meanings of truth and brings them forth into the light for human beings; for when one man draws out this sense, and another that sense, while expounding it in Catholic fashion, it becomes known how lofty and deep it is. Therefore let no man swollen with secular learning suppose that he understands sacred Scripture, unless he first lays aside the veil of pride and of every disordered desire. For secular learning is of more value for exercising the intellect than for illuminating the understanding toward true wisdom. Therefore without doubt divine Scripture is, to minds purified through the continual exercise of the fear of God and frequent study of reading, both manifest and clear, though to filthy minds, confused by secular wisdom, it seems obscure.

Johannes Trithemius, Eight Questions.

Hence he understands the holy Scriptures well and rightly who, with purified affection, being frequent in the study of them, expounds them as did the one who wrote. For if they are read in another spirit than that by which he is believed to have inspired them to be written, the mind must necessarily be wholly shut away from true understanding. But when we encounter some discordance in them, let us understand that it is only of words, not of meanings; and it arises not by chance but by the ordering providence of God, so that the mind, exercised longer in the Scriptures, may be strengthened and not become altogether sluggish. For the counsel of God cannot be deceived; but the divine Scriptures were written by the counsel of his will. It follows necessarily that they are true and in no way false. They were men by whom the divine [Scriptures] came to us. You who are devoted to secular wisdom, say of the divine Scriptures of the New and Old Testament, which the Church of Christians has received and venerates as true, authentic, and holy Scripture: whence do you believe it was received, from God or from men? If from God, why do you not believe it? For everyone who attacks the Scripture which he believes to be inspired most openly resists the divine ordering. But if it is from men, why do you hope for the eternal salvation promised in it, which man cannot give? Unless perhaps, madmen, you go on to say that all things are fabricated, and that nothing remains after fate except ashes, and that the mind together with the body undergoes

To Maximilian Caesar

destruction, a profession which would show you to be no less insane than foolish. For if you truly believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, you will necessarily say that the divine Scriptures were inspired by the Holy Spirit; but if, having fallen with the apostates into a reprobate sense, you say that they were [composed?] by men, you impiously show how far you are from true wisdom, wandering in darkness, and you openly reveal yourselves to be unskilled and rash judges, since you condemn Scripture which you do not understand. But because it is more familiar to you to despise wisdom than to learn it, it is not the purpose of this work to weary the mind longer against the rashness of emperors. This one thing I want you to know: that no one understands unless he receives; but because you set the filth of your affections in the way, so that you may not receive, therefore you do not have the understanding of true wisdom.
